newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic says Kosovo must stay part of Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic says Kosovo must stay part of Serbia.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Wednesday dashed ethnic Albanian hopes that Serbia might grant independence to its mainly-Albanian province of Kosovo.

"The word Kosovo is being frequently used in pressures exerted against our country... There are no pressures under which we will yield an inch of Kosovo and Metohija," Milosevic told a rally in the main square of Pristina.
Milosevic arrived in Pristina, the Kosovo capital, on an election campaign tour of the troubled province which launched his political career 10 years ago.

"In this respect (yielding Kosovo) there never has been, nor there will be, any discussion, nor should there be any doubt in the outcome of such policy," he told thousands of Serbs and party faithful.
Kosovo, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one, is widely regarded as a political powder keg which, if ignited, could wreck international peace efforts in the Balkans.
But a senior western diplomat based in Belgrade said there was no pressure being exerted on Belgrade to grant Kosovo's independence.
"Kosovo is a part of Serbia. In this matter the United States and Europe think as one," he said.

The United States has made an improvement in Serbia's treatment of Kosovo one of its conditions for lifting remaining sanctions in force against federal Yugoslavia, which consists of Serbia and the tiny republic of Montenegro.
Albanian leaders have mistaken this demand as a green light to demand independence, diplomats said.
Serbia revoked Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, claiming its Albanian population wanted to secede and join neighbouring Albania.

The Albanians have boycotted Serbian institutions since, and their leaders have openly called for secession, forcing the United States to warn them secession was not an option and to find a solution within Serbia.
All Serb-Albanian talks over the past few months to find a solution to the impasse have been deadlocked.
In the meantime the province has been rocked over the past year by a wave of violence in which more than 30 people have been killed, despite a heavy Serbian police and army presence.
Clandestine Albanian organisations have been blamed for the attacks and scores of ethnic Albanians have been sentenced to stiff prison sentences.
Milosevic on Wednesday called for tolerance in the impoverished province.
"National equality must reign in this region, as well as a spirit of tolerance and all features of a humane, developed and democratic society," he said.

Milosevic is expected to replace outgoing Yugoslav President Zoran Lilic, who steps down on Thursday, and assume the federal presidency within weeks, paving the way for presidential elections in Serbia early this autumn.
The Serbian constitution forbids him from seeking a third term as the republic's president.
Milosevic's campaign pitches include reforms and economic development of the country, now emerging from under U.N. sanctions for its involvement in the war in Bosnia.

"We are now in a stage of intensive economic recovery... in the phase of intensive reforms aimed at creating conditions for normal, accelerated development, increased employment, increased wages, living standards," he said.
This should "enable our economy and society to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the most developed European countries by the end of the decade", he said.
